correctness.rationale: Neutral antisymmetric modes split off as a zero direct summand; in the bright block the independently computed quartic is (x²-k)(x²+gamma²-t²)-2x(x+t). A multiple nonreal root would make it a squared real quadratic, contradicting the absent cubic and nonzero linear coefficients. A multiple root at zero is excluded by P'(0)=-2t, and elimination at a positive root would force t<0. Negative repeated roots -u give the stated T_k,G_k. T_k' has just the two stated critical points, with 0<y_k<k and strict decrease between them, so the coupling interval is nonempty and contains exactly three crossings. Their gains are distinct since two negative double roots contradict the zero cubic coefficient; gamma>0, u²!=k and t!=4u³ give transverse double roots. To justify alternation, including the step not explicit in the frozen proof, P(sqrt(k))=-2k-2t sqrt(k)<0 and both tails are positive: there are always at least two real roots, so the phases must alternate 4,2,4,2 starting at the simple Hermitian spectrum. At gamma=t the simple bright zero can coincide only semisimply with dark modes (direct sum). At t=4y_k^(3/2) the quartic factors as (x+sqrt(y_k))³(x-3sqrt(y_k)); G_k(sqrt(y_k))>0, and the indicated rank-three minor is nonzero there and at every positive-gain collision. Each such multiple root therefore has one Jordan block of the claimed size.
residual_risks: This is an exact spectral classification in the given open coupling interval and at a tuned EP3, not a diagram of every coupling. Real eigenvalues at a defective point do not ensure bounded time evolution.

value.rationale: A single closing link changes the spectral behavior of a previously unlinked balanced star. The exact open interval guarantees a second real window despite prior symmetry breaking, and the nonzero-energy Jordan block gives a sharply tunable and analytically checkable higher-order degeneracy. The bright reduction exhibits how spectator modes can affect the active spectrum without changing the dark zero eigenvalues.
residual_risks: An exact finite-dimensional benchmark, not evidence of implementation robustness or a statement for open-system Lindblad dynamics.
